<description>
{
 "summary": "Adds a request completion deadline to Bitcoin Core's HTTP server to disconnect clients that take too long to send a complete request. The deadline is armed when the first byte of a request is received, expires after -rpcservertimeout, and is not extended by subsequent reads. It is cleared once request parsing completes, deferred while worker threads process a request, and restarted while response bytes are actively going out.",
 "problem": "The existing -rpcservertimeout only tracks inactivity between reads. A client trickling bytes indefinitely without completing a request continually resets the idle timer, permanently occupying an HTTP connection slot without ever hitting RPC authentication. Because connection slots are capped by default at 16 (or -rpcmaxconnections), such clients can exhaust all available slots and prevent any legitimate RPC requests from being accepted.",
 "evidence": [
  "The author provides a concrete reproduction: starting a node with -rpcmaxconnections=2, opening two sockets, and trickling 'GET / HTTP/1.1\\r\\n' one byte every ten seconds causes bitcoin-cli getblockcount to hang indefinitely.",
  "Description notes: 'Connection slots are capped by default 16 or by -rpcmaxconnections. Once those slots are taken, the server stops accepting new connections. Because no request ever completes the authentication functions are never hit.'"
 ],

<category name="rpc" title="RPC / REST / ZMQ">
## Covers

The node's programmatic interfaces: JSON-RPC methods and their help and
argument handling, the HTTP server and authentication, `bitcoin-cli`,
the REST interface, and ZMQ notifications. Wallet RPCs are wallet first
and rpc second unless the change is to the RPC machinery itself. The
RPC/REST/ZMQ label is a strong prior.

Not rpc: the behavior an RPC merely exposes (that belongs to its area).

## What matters here

Compatibility first: changes that break or silently alter what existing
callers get back affect every application built on the node, so
correctness of returned data and the discipline around deprecations
matter most. Then security of the interface: authentication, exposure
of sensitive data, resource exhaustion through the HTTP server. Then
gaps that force applications into workarounds: missing fields or
methods that downstream software has asked for, with evidence they
asked. Then performance of hot methods that block explorers and
indexers call constantly. Then consistency and documentation of the
interface.

New methods without an external consumer asking rank low.
